claim: Dictyostelium and mammalian phagocytes share mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
source: The genetic/molecular model Dictyostelium and mammalian phagocytes share mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis and phagocytosis; Dictyostelium chemotax toward bacteria and phagocytose them as food sources.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise for the study, drawing on established scientific knowledge about these organisms.

claim: Dictyostelium chemotax toward bacteria and phagocytose them as food sources.
source: The genetic/molecular model Dictyostelium and mammalian phagocytes share mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis and phagocytosis; Dictyostelium chemotax toward bacteria and phagocytose them as food sources.
evidence: This is stated as a known behavior of Dictyostelium in the abstract.

claim: Dictyostelium demonstrate high sensitivity to multiple bacterially-secreted chemoattractants.
source: We quantified Dictyostelium chemotaxis towards live gram positive and gram negative bacteria and demonstrate high sensitivity to multiple bacterially-secreted chemoattractants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing chemotaxis responses to bacteria.

claim: Intracellular signaling-networks for multiple ligands utilize independent upstream adaptive mechanisms.
source: Additive/competitive assays indicate that intracellular signaling-networks for multiple ligands utilize independent upstream adaptive mechanisms, but common downstream targets, thus amplifying detection at low signal propagation, but strengthening discrimination of multiple inputs.
evidence: This is supported by the additive/competitive assay data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Intracellular signaling-networks for multiple ligands utilize common downstream targets.
source: Additive/competitive assays indicate that intracellular signaling-networks for multiple ligands utilize independent upstream adaptive mechanisms, but common downstream targets, thus amplifying detection at low signal propagation, but strengthening discrimination of multiple inputs.
evidence: This is supported by the additive/competitive assay data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Chemoattractant receptor-signaling is not essential for bacterial phagocytosis.
source: Finally, analyses of signaling-networks for chemotaxis and phagocytosis indicate that chemoattractant receptor-signaling is not essential for bacterial phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 7, 8, and 9 comparing phagocytosis in cells with and without chemoattractant receptors.

claim: Professional phagocytes hunt and destroy bacteria and other small non-related single-celled organisms.
source: Professional phagocytes hunt and destroy bacteria and other small non-related single-celled organisms, and survey for apoptotic or necrotic cells and cell remnants (Boulais et al., 2010; Freeman and Grinstein, 2014; Niedergang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Professional phagocytes survey for apoptotic or necrotic cells and cell remnants.
source: Professional phagocytes hunt and destroy bacteria and other small non-related single-celled organisms, and survey for apoptotic or necrotic cells and cell remnants (Boulais et al., 2010; Freeman and Grinstein, 2014; Niedergang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phagocytic functions originally served to fulfill nutritional requirements.
source: While these functions originally served to fulfill nutritional requirements (Cosson and Soldati, 2008; de Nooijer et al., 2009), they have been re-purposed as a first line innate immune response in the complex metazoan.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phagocytic functions have been re-purposed as a first line innate immune response in the complex metazoan.
source: While these functions originally served to fulfill nutritional requirements (Cosson and Soldati, 2008; de Nooijer et al., 2009), they have been re-purposed as a first line innate immune response in the complex metazoan.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phagocytes that have retained ancient utility for foraging (e.g. Dictyostelium) or display defensive or developmental postures (e.g. macrophages) share common mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
source: Still, phagocytes that have either retained ancient utility for foraging (e.g. Dictyostelium) or display defensive or developmental postures (e.g. macrophages) share common mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis (detection) and phagocytosis (killing), despite their evolutionary separation ~103 myo (Bozzaro et al., 2008; Cosson and Soldati, 2008; Jin et al., 2008; de Nooijer et al., 2009; Bozzaro and Eichinger, 2011; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dictyostelium and macrophages have an evolutionary separation of approximately 103 million years.
source: Still, phagocytes that have either retained ancient utility for foraging (e.g. Dictyostelium) or display defensive or developmental postures (e.g. macrophages) share common mechanistic pathways for chemotaxis (detection) and phagocytosis (killing), despite their evolutionary separation ~103 myo (Bozzaro et al., 2008; Cosson and Soldati, 2008; Jin et al., 2008; de Nooijer et al., 2009; Bozzaro and Eichinger, 2011; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both Dictyostelium and mammalian cells utilize GPCRs for chemoattractant/chemokine detection.
source: Both Dictyostelium and mammalian cells utilize GPCRs (G protein-coupled receptors) for chemoattractant/chemokine detection and related downstream pathways for activation response (e.g. Ras, PKA, PI3K, TORC2, AKT, PDK1, ERKs, Cyclases, Actin (Van Haastert and Veltman, 2007; Jin et al., 2008; McMains et al., 2008; Swaney et al., 2010; Jin, 2013; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dictyostelium and mammalian cells use related downstream pathways for activation response including Ras, PKA, PI3K, TORC2, AKT, PDK1, ERKs, Cyclases, and Actin.
source: Both Dictyostelium and mammalian cells utilize GPCRs (G protein-coupled receptors) for chemoattractant/chemokine detection and related downstream pathways for activation response (e.g. Ras, PKA, PI3K, TORC2, AKT, PDK1, ERKs, Cyclases, Actin (Van Haastert and Veltman, 2007; Jin et al., 2008; McMains et al., 2008; Swaney et al., 2010; Jin, 2013; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chemotaxis/migration of Dictyostelium and mammalian cells are similarly inhibited by latrunculin A, PD 169316, SB 525334, and other small molecules.
source: Chemotaxis/migration of Dictyostelium and mammalian cells are similarly inhibited by latrunculin A, PD 169316, SB 525334, and other small molecules (Liao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Phagocytic processes are highly conserved and mechanistically common to both Dictyostelium and macrophages.
source: Phagocytic processes are also highly conserved and mechanistically common to both Dictyostelium and macrophages (Gotthardt et al., 2006; Bozzaro et al., 2008; Cosson and Soldati, 2008; Boulais et al., 2010; Freeman and Grinstein, 2014; Levin et al., 2016; Niedergang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Particle interaction at the cell surface induces an actin re-organization, forming a cup in the plasma membrane that surrounds the particle for engulfment and re-direction to lysosomes for degradation.
source: Particle interaction at the cell surface induces an actin re-organization, forming a cup in the plasma membrane that surrounds the particle for engulfment and re-direction to lysosomes for degradation.
evidence: This describes a known mechanism of phagocytosis based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cells of the mammalian immune system and Dictyostelium exhibit similar susceptibility to virulence infection by Legionella pneumophila, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Listeria monocytogenes.
source: The shared mechanisms also underscore the great utility for model studies of host-pathogen interactions, where cells of the mammalian immune system and Dictyostelium exhibit similar susceptibility to virulence infection by Legionella pneumophila, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Listeria monocytogenes (Bozzaro et al., 2008; Steinert, 2011; Levin et al., 2016; Gray and Botelho, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Growing Dictyostelium migrate to folate with an EC50 of approximately 5 nM.
source: Under these conditions, growing cells migrate toward folate with an EC50 ~5 nM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The calculated EC50 for folate chemotaxis defines a very high detection/migration sensitivity of less than 0.5 nM.
source: While we recognize that this is a calculated maximum for cell exposure to folate, it defines a very high detection/migration sensitivity (<0.5 nM) and emphasizes the robust nature for chemotaxis in this assay.
evidence: This is inferred from the EC50 data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells lacking Gβ are completely unresponsive to folate.
source: Cells lacking Gβ, an essential subunit for all receptor/G protein signaling (Wu et al., 1995; Peracino et al., 1998; Hoeller et al., 2016) were completely unresponsive to folate (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations to published literature.

claim: Gβ is an essential subunit for all receptor/G protein signaling.
source: Cells lacking Gβ, an essential subunit for all receptor/G protein signaling (Wu et al., 1995; Peracino et al., 1998; Hoeller et al., 2016) were completely unresponsive to folate (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gα4 is generally considered essential for most folate responses.
source: Gα4 is generally considered essential for most folate responses, although limited, compensatory actions by other Gα proteins have been suggested (Natarajan et al., 2000); chemotaxis to folate is significantly reduced in cells lacking Gα4, but chemotaxis may not be eliminated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Chemotaxis to folate is significantly reduced in cells lacking Gα4, but chemotaxis may not be eliminated.
source: Gα4 is generally considered essential for most folate responses, although limited, compensatory actions by other Gα proteins have been suggested (Natarajan et al., 2000); chemotaxis to folate is significantly reduced in cells lacking Gα4, but chemotaxis may not be eliminated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cells lacking Gα2 migrate to folate as robustly as do WT.
source: In contrast, cells lacking Gα2, a cAMP receptor-coupled G protein subunit (Kumagai et al., 1989), migrate to folate as robustly as do WT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gα2 is a cAMP receptor-coupled G protein subunit.
source: In contrast, cells lacking Gα2, a cAMP receptor-coupled G protein subunit (Kumagai et al., 1989), migrate to folate as robustly as do WT.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GrlL was recently defined as a GPCR for folate (fAR1).
source: The orphan receptor GrlL (Hereld, 2005; Basu et al., 2013) was recently defined as a GPCR for folate [fAR1 (Pan et al., 2016)], a conclusion that we have separately confirmed by comprehensive analyses of GPCRs expressed in growing Dictyostelium (NPM and ARK, in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and confirmed by the authors' own unpublished work.

claim: Cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 are unable to chemotax specifically to folate.
source: Cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 are unable to chemotax specifically to folate, in comparison to buffer controls [(Pan et al., 2016, Figure 1D)], whereas, car1-null cells that lack CAR1, the primary receptor for secreted cAMP and developmental chemotaxis (McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2015), respond robustly to folate signals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to published literature.

claim: CAR1 is the primary receptor for secreted cAMP and developmental chemotaxis.
source: Cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 are unable to chemotax specifically to folate, in comparison to buffer controls [(Pan et al., 2016, Figure 1D)], whereas, car1-null cells that lack CAR1, the primary receptor for secreted cAMP and developmental chemotaxis (McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2015), respond robustly to folate signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: car1-null cells respond robustly to folate signals.
source: Cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 are unable to chemotax specifically to folate, in comparison to buffer controls [(Pan et al., 2016, Figure 1D)], whereas, car1-null cells that lack CAR1, the primary receptor for secreted cAMP and developmental chemotaxis (McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2015), respond robustly to folate signals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dictyostelium exhibited a precise dose-response to bacterial numbers.
source: Dictyostelium exhibited a precise dose-response to bacterial numbers (Figure 2A), as parallel to folate sensing (see Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Even at the limit of the system (~5 × 10^7 bacteria/well), chemotaxis was not saturated.
source: However, even at the limit of the system (~5 × 107 bacteria/well), chemotaxis was not saturated; calculations suggest that >5×109 bacteria/well would be required (see below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and calculations.

claim: Dictyostelium lacking the essential Gβ subunit for GPCR function were completely insensitive to Bacillus.
source: Dictyostelium lacking the essential Gβ subunit for GPCR function were completely insensitive to the Bacillus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus was observed in cells lacking the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit.
source: Further, we observed only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus lacking the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit (Figure 2B), whereas Gα2-null Dictyostelium were fully responsive (Figure 2B), suggesting that folate is the primary Bacillus subtilis chemoattractant (see below, Figures 5A and 7C) sensed by Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gα2-null Dictyostelium were fully responsive to Bacillus.
source: Further, we observed only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus lacking the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit (Figure 2B), whereas Gα2-null Dictyostelium were fully responsive (Figure 2B), suggesting that folate is the primary Bacillus subtilis chemoattractant (see below, Figures 5A and 7C) sensed by Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Folate is the primary Bacillus subtilis chemoattractant sensed by Dictyostelium.
source: Further, we observed only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus lacking the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit (Figure 2B), whereas Gα2-null Dictyostelium were fully responsive (Figure 2B), suggesting that folate is the primary Bacillus subtilis chemoattractant (see below, Figures 5A and 7C) sensed by Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 2B, 5A, and 7C.

claim: The dose response to Klebsiella planticola was in a similar range to that of Bacillus subtilis.
source: Interestingly the dose response to Klebsiella planticola was in a similar range to that of Bacillus subtilis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: Dictyostelium that lack either the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit or the cAMP-responsive Gα2 remained partially sensitive to Klebsiella.
source: Surprisingly however, Dictyostelium that lack either the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit or the cAMP-responsive Gα2 remained partially sensitive to Klebsiella (Figure 2D), suggesting that both folate and cAMP contribute to directional sensing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both folate and cAMP contribute to directional sensing of Klebsiella.
source: Surprisingly however, Dictyostelium that lack either the folate-responsive Gα4 subunit or the cAMP-responsive Gα2 remained partially sensitive to Klebsiella (Figure 2D), suggesting that both folate and cAMP contribute to directional sensing.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Chemotactic migration of growth-phase Dictyostelium to cAMP has not been previously observed.
source: Although growing Dictyostelium express low levels of the chemoattractant receptor for cAMP, chemotactic migration of growth-phase Dictyostelium to cAMP has not been previously observed (Veltman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dictyostelium secretes cAMP during development and responds chemotactically to promote cell aggregation at centers of cAMP signaling.
source: Dictyostelium secretes cAMP during development and responds chemotactically to promote cell aggregation at centers of cAMP signaling (McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Growth-phase WT Dictyostelium exhibit rapid, robust, and highly sensitive migration to cAMP with an EC50 of approximately 6 nM.
source: Interestingly, we detect rapid, robust, and highly sensitive migration of growth-phase WT Dictyostelium to cAMP (Figure 3A,B; EC50 ~6 nM).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The cell population chemotactic to cAMP is similarly chemotactic to folate, indicating they had not undergone a developmental shift from folate to cAMP response.
source: This identical cell population is similarly chemotactic to folate (see below), indicating that they had not undergone a developmental shift from folate to cAMP response.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data comparing chemotaxis to both folate and cAMP.

claim: Cells lacking Gβ or Gα2 do not chemotax to cAMP.
source: Cells lacking Gβ or Gα2 do not chemotax to cAMP, whereas cells lacking the folate-specific Gα4 are extremely responsive to cAMP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells lacking the folate-specific Gα4 are extremely responsive to cAMP.
source: Cells lacking Gβ or Gα2 do not chemotax to cAMP, whereas cells lacking the folate-specific Gα4 are extremely responsive to cAMP (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 show robust chemotactic response to cAMP.
source: In a reciprocal analysis of CAR1 and GrlL/fAR1 for cAMP detection, cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 show robust chemotactic response, whereas chemotaxis of car1-null cells to cAMP is extremely suppressed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chemotaxis of car1-null cells to cAMP is extremely suppressed.
source: In a reciprocal analysis of CAR1 and GrlL/fAR1 for cAMP detection, cells lacking GrlL/fAR1 show robust chemotactic response, whereas chemotaxis of car1-null cells to cAMP is extremely suppressed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At sub-optimal (<50 nM) concentrations, folate and cAMP exhibit enhanced effects compared to either chemoattractant alone.
source: At sub-optimal (<50 nM) concentrations, folate and cAMP exhibit enhanced effects compared to either chemoattractant alone (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a near-maximal dose (~500 nM) of either folate or cAMP is applied, only minimal additional chemotaxis is observed when a second chemoattractant is included.
source: However, these effects may not be strictly additive. When a near-maximal dose (i.e. ~500 nM) of either folate or cAMP (see Figures 1C and 3B) is applied, only minimal additional chemotaxis is observed when a second chemoattractant is included (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The folate and cAMP pathways act, at least partially, through common rate-limiting, downstream components for chemotaxis.
source: Thus, the folate and cAMP pathways act, at least partially, through common rate-limiting, downstream components for chemotaxis (see Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the additive assay data and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When cells are exposed to saturating doses of a chemoattractant, their response pathways adapt and cells become insensitive for directed migration or biochemical activation, regardless of the gradient profile.
source: When cells are exposed to saturating doses of a chemoattractant, their response pathways adapt and cells become insensitive for directed migration or biochemical activation, regardless of the gradient profile (McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014; Nichols et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cells plated in the presence of saturating folate are inhibited from migrating toward non-saturating folate in the bottom well.
source: Thus, when cells (in the upper chamber) are plated in the presence of a saturating (5 μM) folate dose, they are inhibited from migrating toward non-saturating (50 nM) folate in the bottom well (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Folate-adapted cells remain chemotactically responsive to low doses of cAMP.
source: However, these folate-adapted cells, in the upper chamber, remain chemotactically responsive to low doses of cAMP in the bottom well.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells plated in the presence of saturating cAMP do not migrate toward cAMP in the bottom well, but continue to chemotax to folate.
source: When the folate and cAMP treatments are reversed, we observed a reciprocal effect. Cells plated in the presence of saturating cAMP, in the upper chamber, do not migrate toward cAMP in the bottom well, but continue to chemotax to folate (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), with perhaps slightly enhanced sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adaptation pathways for folate and cAMP function independently of one another and upstream of common downstream effector systems.
source: These results support our previous conclusions, based on biochemical experiments (Liao et al., 2013), that adaptation pathways for folate and cAMP function independently of one another and upstream of common downstream effector systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive assay data and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The addition of folate or cAMP to cells in the upper chamber does not elicit a significant increase in basal motility via ligand-activated chemokinesis.
source: As a further control, we show that the addition of folate or cAMP to cells in the upper chamber does not elicit a significant increase in basal motility, via ligand-activated chemokinesis (Varnum and Soll, 1984; Kriebel et al., 2003), to alter random movement toward a buffer control in the bottom well (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citations to published literature.

claim: Only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus was observed in WT Dictyostelium using folate as a competitor.
source: We observed only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus of WT Dictyostelium using folate as a competitor, whereas WT cells plated in the presence of competing cAMP were fully responsive (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WT cells plated in the presence of competing cAMP were fully responsive to Bacillus.
source: We observed only minimal chemotaxis to Bacillus of WT Dictyostelium using folate as a competitor, whereas WT cells plated in the presence of competing cAMP were fully responsive (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Competition by either folate or cAMP only partially inhibited chemotaxis of WT Dictyostelium to Klebsiella.
source: In contrast, competition by either folate or cAMP in the upper well only partially inhibited chemotaxis of WT Dictyostelium to Klebsiella (Figure 5B), confirming that both folate and cAMP contribute to directional sensing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No pERK2 activation was observed at zero-time, confirming that chemoattractants were not carried over from bacterial growth media.
source: No pERK2 activation was observed at zero-time, confirming that chemoattractants were not carried over from bacterial growth media (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A time-dependent increase in chemoattractant-stimulated pERK2 was observed through 120 min of bacterial incubation.
source: However, a time-dependent increase in chemoattractant-simulated pERK2 was observed through 120 min of bacterial incubation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 5 × 10^7 Klebsiella cells secrete and accumulate approximately 20-30 nM cAMP in 2 hours.
source: Using an imunoassay to quantify cAMP, we show the secretion and accumulation of ~20–30 nM cAMP by 5 × 107 Klebsiella cells in 2 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using an immunoassay.

claim: cAMP secretion by Bacillus was not detected in a direct immunoassay.
source: In addition, we were unable to detect cAMP secretion by Bacillus in a direct immunoassay, supporting our previous conclusions that cAMP was not a significant chemoattractant for Bacillus sensing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using an immunoassay.

claim: A density-dependent level of secreted chemoattractants was observed from different numbers of Klebsiella planticola.
source: To further correlate chemoattractant secretion to cellular response, we also assayed pERK2 activation using supernatants from different numbers of Klebsiella planticola. We observed the expected density-dependent level of secreted chemoattractants (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 5 × 10^6 Klebsiella planticola elicit a robust chemotactic response but are unable to support pERK2 activation.
source: Interesting, although 5 × 106 Klebsiella planticola will elicit a robust chemotactic response (see Figure 2C), they were unable to support pERK2 activation (Figure 6B), suggesting that chemotactic responses are more sensitive to activation than are individual biochemical pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 6B.

claim: Chemotactic responses are more sensitive to activation than are individual biochemical pathways.
source: Interesting, although 5 × 106 Klebsiella planticola will elicit a robust chemotactic response (see Figure 2C), they were unable to support pERK2 activation (Figure 6B), suggesting that chemotactic responses are more sensitive to activation than are individual biochemical pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 6B.

claim: For folate, the EC50 for pPKBR1 and pERK2 are identical, approximately 45 nM.
source: For folate, the EC50 for pPKBR1 and pERK2 are identical, ~45 nM, which is lower than previously noted but very similar to that of cAMP (EC50 ~20/30/30 nM for pPKBR1/pERK2), when assayed simultaneously (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For cAMP, the EC50 is approximately 20/30/30 nM for pPKBR1/pERK2.
source: For folate, the EC50 for pPKBR1 and pERK2 are identical, ~45 nM, which is lower than previously noted but very similar to that of cAMP (EC50 ~20/30/30 nM for pPKBR1/pERK2), when assayed simultaneously (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For both cAMP and folate, Dictyostelium are 5-10 times more sensitive for chemotactic migration than for biochemical pathway stimulations.
source: Nonetheless, for both cAMP and folate, Dictyostelium are 5–10 times more sensitive for chemotactic migration than for these biochemical pathway stimulations, consistent with chemotactic and bacterial responses for bacterial sensing (Figures 2A, C, 6A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing chemotaxis data (Figures 1C, 3B) with biochemical data (Figure 6C).

claim: PIP3-signaling, via localized PI3K activation, may be associated with chemotaxis, macropinocytosis, and phagocytosis.
source: Although PIP3-signaling, via localized PI3K activation, may be associated with each (Servant et al., 2000; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015; Hoeller et al., 2016) and required for macropinocytosis (Posor et al., 2013; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015), the pathway seems largely dispensable for both chemotaxis and phagocytosis of bacteria (Hoeller and Kay, 2007; Hoeller et al., 2013; Schlam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PIP3-signaling is required for macropinocytosis.
source: Although PIP3-signaling, via localized PI3K activation, may be associated with each (Servant et al., 2000; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015; Hoeller et al., 2016) and required for macropinocytosis (Posor et al., 2013; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015), the pathway seems largely dispensable for both chemotaxis and phagocytosis of bacteria (Hoeller and Kay, 2007; Hoeller et al., 2013; Schlam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The PIP3 pathway seems largely dispensable for both chemotaxis and phagocytosis of bacteria.
source: Although PIP3-signaling, via localized PI3K activation, may be associated with each (Servant et al., 2000; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015; Hoeller et al., 2016) and required for macropinocytosis (Posor et al., 2013; Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015), the pathway seems largely dispensable for both chemotaxis and phagocytosis of bacteria (Hoeller and Kay, 2007; Hoeller et al., 2013; Schlam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bacterial-dependent growth rates of Dictyostelium lacking the folate receptor are only reduced by 20% over the long-term compared to WT cells.
source: However, bacterial-dependent growth rates, in shaking culture, of Dictyostelium lacking the folate receptor are only reduced by 20% over the long-term compared to WT cells (Pan et al., 2016), making a functional connection between folate receptor activation and phagocytosis unclear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WT cells display rapid efficient phagocytosis, as measured by accumulation of total fluorescence through time.
source: WT cells display rapid efficient phagocytosis, as measured by accumulation of total fluorescence through time (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells lacking Gβ exhibit only a minimal time-dependent increase in fluorescence during phagocytosis.
source: Although cells lacking Gβ, a factor that had been previously defined as essential for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Peracino et al., 1998), exhibit only a minimal time-dependent increase in fluorescence, we did not observe a significant inhibition for phagocytosis in cells lacking Gα4, potentially suggesting that folate sensing is not a primary factor for phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Gβ had been previously defined as essential for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium.
source: Although cells lacking Gβ, a factor that had been previously defined as essential for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Peracino et al., 1998), exhibit only a minimal time-dependent increase in fluorescence, we did not observe a significant inhibition for phagocytosis in cells lacking Gα4, potentially suggesting that folate sensing is not a primary factor for phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: No significant inhibition for phagocytosis was observed in cells lacking Gα4.
source: Although cells lacking Gβ, a factor that had been previously defined as essential for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Peracino et al., 1998), exhibit only a minimal time-dependent increase in fluorescence, we did not observe a significant inhibition for phagocytosis in cells lacking Gα4, potentially suggesting that folate sensing is not a primary factor for phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Folate sensing is not a primary factor for phagocytosis.
source: Although cells lacking Gβ, a factor that had been previously defined as essential for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium (Peracino et al., 1998), exhibit only a minimal time-dependent increase in fluorescence, we did not observe a significant inhibition for phagocytosis in cells lacking Gα4, potentially suggesting that folate sensing is not a primary factor for phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: grlL/far1-null cells and GrlL/fAR1-expressing rescued cells do not show significant differences in the rates of phagocytosis of pHrodo-labelled E. coli.
source: We do not observe significant differences in the rates of phagocytosis of pHrodo-labelled E. coli between grlL/far1-null and the GrlL/fAR1-expressing rescued cells (Figure 7B); likewise, car1-nulls and CAR1-expressing cells exhibit identical phagocytic properties (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: car1-nulls and CAR1-expressing cells exhibit identical phagocytic properties.
source: We do not observe significant differences in the rates of phagocytosis of pHrodo-labelled E. coli between grlL/far1-null and the GrlL/fAR1-expressing rescued cells (Figure 7B); likewise, car1-nulls and CAR1-expressing cells exhibit identical phagocytic properties (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Phagocytosis per se is not substantially regulated by chemoattractant receptors nor is it markedly influenced by their dependent downstream activations.
source: These data indicate that phagocytosis per se is not substantially regulated by chemoattractant receptors nor is it markedly influenced by their dependent downstream activations.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: GrlL/fAR1-expressing cells chemotax to labeled B. subtilis, whereas the grlL/far1-nulls were completely insensitive.
source: GrlL/fAR1-expressing cells chemotax to labeled B. subtilis, whereas the grlL/far1-nulls were completely insensitive. Yet, both cell lines exhibit identical parameters for phagocytosis, thus separating an essential GrlL/fAR1 dependency for chemotaxis to folate-secreting cells, from a functional role in phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: grlL/far1-null and GrlL/fAR1-expressing cells exhibit identical parameters for phagocytosis of labeled B. subtilis.
source: GrlL/fAR1-expressing cells chemotax to labeled B. subtilis, whereas the grlL/far1-nulls were completely insensitive. Yet, both cell lines exhibit identical parameters for phagocytosis, thus separating an essential GrlL/fAR1 dependency for chemotaxis to folate-secreting cells, from a functional role in phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The folate GPCR is essential for chemotaxis to folate-secreting bacteria, but does not appear to have a significant function in the phagocytosis of these same bacteria.
source: Although the folate GPCR is essential for chemotaxis to folate-secreting bacteria, this receptor does not appear to have a significant function in the phagocytosis of these same bacteria.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No differences in phagocytic rates were observed in WT cells stimulated with cAMP or folate compared to non-stimulated controls.
source: No differences in phagocytic rates were observed, regardless of treatment (Figure 8), indicating that chemotactic-activation does not inherently potentiate cells for phagocytic functions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Chemotactic-activation does not inherently potentiate cells for phagocytic functions.
source: No differences in phagocytic rates were observed, regardless of treatment (Figure 8), indicating that chemotactic-activation does not inherently potentiate cells for phagocytic functions.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: WT and grlL/far1-null cells show identical rates of phagocytosis to pHrodo-beads.
source: WT and grlL/far1-null cells show identical rates of phagocytosis to pHrodo-beads (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There is a near 100% coordinate labeling of pHrodo and Folate-FITC fluorescence markers at the bead surfaces.
source: We estimate that each bead displays, on average, ~20,000 folate surface ligands and there is a near 100% coordinate labeling of pHrodo and Folate-FITC fluorescence markers at the bead surfaces (see Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Identical rates of phagocytosis were observed with WT cells using either pHrodo- or Folate-FITC/pHrodo-beads as a substrate.
source: Identical rates of phagocytosis were observed with WT cells using either pHrodo- or Folate-FITC/pHrodo-beads as a substrate (Figure 9B), indicating that WT cells, which express folate receptors, do not differentially recognize folate-coated from non-coated beads for functional phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: WT cells, which express folate receptors, do not differentially recognize folate-coated from non-coated beads for functional phagocytosis.
source: Identical rates of phagocytosis were observed with WT cells using either pHrodo- or Folate-FITC/pHrodo-beads as a substrate (Figure 9B), indicating that WT cells, which express folate receptors, do not differentially recognize folate-coated from non-coated beads for functional phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: WT cells and cells lacking the chemotaxis folate receptor phagocytose Folate-FITC/pHrodo-beads with identical facility.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that WT cells and cells lacking the chemotaxis folate receptor phagocytose Folate-FITC/pHrodo-beads with identical facility (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Chemo-sensing of ligands on particle surfaces does not significantly contribute to phagocytic processes.
source: These data further indicate that chemo-sensing of ligands on particle surfaces does not significantly contribute to phagocytic processes.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The secretion and accumulation of chemoattractant de-activating enzymes (deaminase for folate; PDE for cAMP) by Dictyostelium serve to attenuate signal levels in close cellular proximity, thereby strengthening the concentration of the gradient and reinforcing directional migration.
source: The secretion and accumulation of chemoattractant de-activating enzymes (deaminase for folate; PDE for cAMP) by Dictyostelium serve to attenuate signal levels in close cellular proximity, thereby strengthening the concentration of the gradient and reinforcing directional migration (Mackenzie et al., 2016; Tweedy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At least 6 signaling arms are activated downstream of chemoattractant receptors in Dictyostelium.
source: At least 6 signaling arms are activated downstream of chemoattractant receptors in Dictyostelium (Van Haastert and Veltman, 2007; McMains et al., 2008; Artemenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The collective and coordinated activities of multiple signaling paths are sufficient to initiate directed migration at <0.5 nM, even though low level chemoattractant stimulation may be too weak to be detectable in an individual biochemical read-out.
source: Although low level (e.g. 1 nM) chemoattractant stimulation may elicit too weak a response to be detectable in an individual biochemical read-out, the collective and coordinated activities of multiple signaling paths are sufficient to initiate directed migration, at <0.5 nM.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of chemotaxis and biochemical assay sensitivities.

claim: Chemotactic signaling networks are shared among Dictyostelium, macrophages, and neutrophils.
source: Since chemotactic signaling networks are shared among Dictyostelium, macrophages, and neutrophils, it is likely that similar interplays function during immune response to ensure high sensitivity for chemotaxis.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about these organisms.

claim: Similar interplays likely function during immune response to ensure high sensitivity for chemotaxis.
source: Since chemotactic signaling networks are shared among Dictyostelium, macrophages, and neutrophils, it is likely that similar interplays function during immune response to ensure high sensitivity for chemotaxis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the shared mechanisms.

claim: Bacterial detection may be further enhanced under conditions of even more limited signal production, where phagocytes migrate toward multiple bacterially-secreted chemoattractants that can act cooperatively at low concentrations.
source: We suggest that bacterial detection may be further enhanced under conditions of even more limited (e.g. 0.1 nM) signal production, where phagocytes migrate toward multiple bacterially-secreted chemoattractants that can act cooperatively at low concentrations.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings.

claim: At very high concentrations (>100 μM), Dictyostelium chemotaxis is diminished.
source: At the other end of the concentration spectrum (>100 μM), Dictyostelium chemotaxis is diminished (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: At very high chemoattractant concentrations, there is ligand-specific down regulation of GrlL/fAR1 and CAR1 protein and mRNA expression.
source: At these concentrations, there is ligand-specific down regulation of GrlL/fAR1 (NPM and ARK, in preparation) and CAR1 protein and mRNA expression (Kimmel, 1987; Klein et al., 1987; Louis et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and unpublished data.

claim: Reduced chemotaxis of growing Dictyostelium toward areas of very high chemoattractant concentration may be an avoidance measure, since Dictyostelium have reduced viability in the presence of extreme bacterial density.
source: We suggest that reduced chemotaxis of growing Dictyostelium toward areas of very high chemoattractant concentration may be an avoidance measure, since Dictyostelium have reduced viability in the presence of extreme bacterial density [(Nasser et al., 2013) NPM and ARK, in preparation].
evidence: This is speculated based on experimental observations and citations.

claim: Cells that have become desensitized through ligand saturation by one chemoattractant remain fully responsive to activation by other bacterially secreted chemoattractants.
source: However, cells that have become desensitized though ligand saturation by one chemoattractant (Wu and Lin, 2011; Liao et al., 2013), remain fully responsive to activation by other bacterially secreted chemoattractants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature.

claim: Activations by low-dose stimulation with multiple chemoattractants will amplify gradient detection and low density bacterial sensing.
source: Activations by low-dose stimulation with multiple chemoattracts will amplify gradient detection and low density bacterial sensing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings on additive effects.

claim: PIP3 membrane patches have been shown to co-localize with phagocytic cups.
source: Similarly, PIP3 membrane patches have been shown to co-localize with phagocytic cups (Hoeller et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In WT, PIP3-free pseudopods primarily orient towards folate during migration.
source: In WT, PIP3-free pseudopods primarily orient towards folate during migration (Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015), suggesting that if PIP3-labeled cellular protrusions participate in phagocytic cup formation, they are not initiated via folate signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: If PIP3-labeled cellular protrusions participate in phagocytic cup formation, they are not initiated via folate signaling.
source: In WT, PIP3-free pseudopods primarily orient towards folate during migration (Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015), suggesting that if PIP3-labeled cellular protrusions participate in phagocytic cup formation, they are not initiated via folate signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from citations to published literature.

claim: Macropinocytosis is functionally antagonistic to chemotaxis.
source: Macropinocytosis, a process for fluid-phase uptake that requires PI3K/PIP3-signaling (Hoeller et al., 2013; Posor et al., 2013), is functionally antagonistic to chemotaxis (Veltman et al., 2014; Veltman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PIP3 production interferes with pseudopod orientation during chemotaxis of growing cells to folate.
source: Thus, PIP3 production interferes with pseudopod orientation during chemotaxis of growing cells to folate, further disconnecting PI3K/PIP3-signaling from chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from citations to published literature.

claim: Phagocytic cup and chemotaxis leading edge formation are competitive events.
source: Indeed, in other processes phagocytic cup and chemotaxis leading edge formation are competitive events (Maniak et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Efficient phagocytosis is independent of chemo-sensing and chemotaxis.
source: Our data demonstrate efficient phagocytosis that is independent of chemo-sensing and chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7, 8, and 9.

claim: Other approaches using mammalian neutrophils have defined incubation conditions that will suppress chemotaxis without affecting phagocytosis.
source: Other approaches using mammalian neutrophils have also defined incubation conditions that will suppress chemotaxis without affecting phagocytosis (Heinrich and Lee, 2011; Mankovich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Chemotactically active neutrophils are more efficient in blocking the growth of infective fungi, subsequent to phagocytosis.
source: It is also suggested that chemotactically active neutrophils are more efficient in blocking the growth of infective fungi, subsequent to phagocytosis (Jones et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The system can be used to examine virulent and non-virulent bacterial strains, search for novel chemoattractants and their orphan receptors, and screen for molecular inhibitors of chemotaxis/phagocytosis.
source: The system was extended to investigate interdependencies of chemotaxis and phagocytosis and can be used to examine virulent and non-virulent bacterial strains, search for novel chemoattractants and their orphan receptors, and screen for molecular inhibitors of chemotaxis/phagocytosis, and further applied to macrophages, neutrophils, as well as Dictyostelium.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential application of the system.
